title: Array or linked list: which should you choose?
answer: Arrays store indexed elements with good locality. Linked lists store nodes with links; they trade index access and extra allocation for convenient splicing when a node and its predecessor are already known.
example: Use an array for a scoreboard read by rank; a list can help splice a known work item.
pitfall: Saying linked-list deletion is always constant time ignores finding the node.
followUp: How would the choice change when most operations are iteration?

complexity.time: Array access O(1), middle insert O(n); list lookup O(n), known-node splice O(1)
complexity.space: Array storage O(n); list storage O(n) including links
complexity.notes: n is the number of elements; singly linked deletion needs the predecessor.

title: Why is ArrayList append amortized O(1)?
answer: Most appends write into unused capacity. Occasionally a larger buffer must be allocated and existing elements copied; spread across geometrically growing capacity, total copying over n appends is linear.
example: Appending one million items does not copy a million items on every append.
pitfall: Amortized is not the same as average over randomly distributed inputs.
followUp: When would reserving capacity help?

complexity.time: Append amortized O(1), individual growth O(n)
complexity.space: O(n) stored capacity; resizing temporarily needs another buffer
complexity.notes: Assume geometric growth and constant-cost reference copies.

title: What is a stack and when is it useful?
answer: A stack removes the most recently added item first. It represents unfinished nested work, such as matching brackets or undo operations; in Java, ArrayDeque is a common single-threaded choice.
example: Push each opening bracket and match each closing bracket against the top.
pitfall: Popping without checking for an empty stack can hide invalid input.
followUp: How would you implement a minimum stack?

complexity.time: Push/pop amortized O(1); bracket scan O(n)
complexity.space: O(n) auxiliary space for unmatched brackets
complexity.notes: n is the number of characters; deque resizing can cost O(n) once.

title: How does a queue differ from a stack?
answer: A queue removes the earliest enqueued item first. It supports breadth-first work and buffering, while a stack explores the newest work first.
example: Process tree nodes level by level with a queue.
pitfall: Using ArrayList.remove(0) shifts elements on every removal.
followUp: How would a bounded blocking queue handle a slow consumer?

complexity.time: ArrayDeque enqueue/dequeue amortized O(1)
complexity.notes: w is the maximum queue size; this excludes consumer processing.

title: How does a hash table find a key?
answer: A hash chooses a bucket and equality identifies the matching key within it. Good hash distribution keeps buckets short; resizing maintains load but occasionally moves many entries.
example: Store customer ID to customer record for exact lookups.
pitfall: A hash collision does not mean two keys are equal.
followUp: Why must a key's hash-relevant state stay stable?

complexity.time: Expected get/put O(1); worst-case lookup O(n) in a general chained table
complexity.notes: Assume constant-cost hash/equality; Java tree bins are an implementation-specific mitigation, not a universal hash-table guarantee.

title: When should you use a set instead of a map?
answer: A set represents membership and uniqueness. A map associates each key with a value; choose it when you need counts, metadata or a lookup result rather than only presence.
example: Use a set for visited IDs and a map for visit counts.
pitfall: A set removes duplicates but does not inherently preserve order.
followUp: How would you preserve encounter order?

complexity.time: Hash-based membership expected O(1); processing n values expected O(n)
complexity.notes: u is the number of unique keys; hashing/equality costs are excluded.

title: What invariant makes a binary search tree useful?
answer: Every left subtree contains smaller keys and every right subtree larger keys according to a consistent comparator. Search follows one branch; balancing keeps height logarithmic.
example: Use a balanced ordered map for predecessor and range queries.
pitfall: An ordinary BST built from sorted input can become a chain.
followUp: How do duplicates affect your invariant?

complexity.time: Search/insert O(h); balanced O(log n), unbalanced worst O(n)
complexity.space: O(n) tree storage; iterative search O(1) auxiliary
complexity.notes: h is tree height; comparator calls are assumed constant time.

title: What does a binary heap guarantee?
answer: A min-heap guarantees each parent is no greater than its children, so the root is the minimum. It does not keep siblings or the full backing array sorted.
example: Maintain the largest k stream values using a min-heap of size k.
pitfall: Iteration over PriorityQueue does not produce sorted order.
followUp: Why is heap construction faster than repeated insertion?

complexity.time: Peek O(1), insert/remove root O(log n), bottom-up build O(n)
complexity.space: O(n) storage; sift operations O(1) auxiliary when iterative
complexity.notes: n is heap size; arbitrary element search remains O(n).

title: Adjacency list or adjacency matrix?
answer: Lists store only present edges and suit sparse graphs. A matrix stores every possible pair and makes edge existence cheap, but scans a full row to enumerate neighbors.
example: Road networks are usually sparse; a tiny dense compatibility graph may suit a matrix.
pitfall: Calling every graph operation O(V + E) ignores representation.
followUp: How would you represent weighted directed edges?

complexity.time: List traversal O(V + E); matrix traversal O(V²); matrix edge lookup O(1)
complexity.notes: V is vertices, E is stored directed edges; undirected lists typically store each edge twice.

title: How does a trie support prefix search?
answer: Each step follows one character, sharing prefix nodes across words. Reaching a prefix node locates its subtree; enumerating suggestions still costs the size of the output.
example: Autocomplete for words beginning with inter.
pitfall: Prefix lookup is not the same cost as returning every matching word.
followUp: How would compressed edges reduce memory?

complexity.time: Prefix lookup O(p); suggestions O(p + visited output subtree)
complexity.notes: p is prefix length; child lookup is constant for a fixed alphabet or expected constant with hashing.

title: Design an LRU cache with efficient operations.
answer: Combine a key-to-node hash map with a doubly linked recency list. On access move the node to the front; on insertion beyond capacity unlink the tail and remove its key.
example: Capacity two: access A, B, A, then insert C; evict B.
pitfall: A concurrent map alone cannot make map/list updates atomic.
followUp: How would TTL expiration interact with recency?

complexity.time: Expected O(1) get/put/evict
complexity.notes: c is cache capacity; assumes expected O(1) hashing and excludes locking contention.

title: What problems does disjoint-set union solve?
answer: It tracks connected components while edges are added. Union by rank or size plus path compression avoids repeatedly walking long parent chains.
example: Detect whether a new undirected edge joins two already connected vertices.
pitfall: It does not efficiently undo arbitrary deletions or return a path between vertices.
followUp: What changes for offline dynamic connectivity?

complexity.time: Amortized O(α(n)) per union/find with both optimizations
complexity.notes: α is inverse Ackermann; this is an amortized bound, not strict O(1).

title: Why use a monotonic deque for sliding-window maximum?
answer: Keep candidate indices in decreasing value order. Remove expired indices from the front and smaller candidates from the back; each index enters and leaves at most once.
example: For window size three, track the largest of each consecutive triple.
pitfall: Storing only values makes duplicate expiration harder to handle correctly.
followUp: How does this differ from a monotonic stack?

complexity.time: O(n) total time
complexity.notes: n is input length; k is window width; each index is inserted and removed at most once.

title: HashMap or TreeMap for ordered queries?
answer: HashMap suits exact lookups. TreeMap maintains comparator order and supports floor, ceiling and sorted ranges, paying a logarithmic update cost.
example: Find the most recent price at or before a timestamp with floorEntry.
pitfall: A comparator returning zero treats keys as equivalent even when equals differs.
followUp: What happens if comparator order disagrees with equals?

complexity.time: TreeMap get/put/remove O(log n); range iteration O(log n + r)
complexity.notes: r is returned entries; assume constant-cost comparisons.

title: What does an immutable data structure buy you?
answer: Readers can share a stable snapshot without defensive locking around mutations. Persistent structures can share unchanged nodes, but immutability alone does not specify operation costs.
example: Publish a new configuration snapshot while existing requests retain the old one.
pitfall: An unmodifiable wrapper is not a deep immutable copy of its elements.
followUp: How would you safely publish a snapshot between threads?

complexity.time: Copy-on-write array update O(n); path-copy balanced tree update O(log n)
complexity.space: O(n) copy or O(log n) new tree nodes per update
complexity.notes: Bounds depend on the chosen representation, not the word immutable.

title: What do Big O, Θ and Ω mean?
answer: Big O is an asymptotic upper bound, Ω a lower bound and Θ a tight bound in a stated cost model. Specify worst case, expected or amortized separately; the notation alone does not choose a case.
example: A complete array scan is Θ(n) even though O(n²) is also a loose upper bound.
pitfall: Big O is not a stopwatch measurement or automatically the worst case.
followUp: Why can an O(n²) algorithm win for tiny inputs?

complexity.time: Full scan Θ(n)
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary for a running sum
complexity.notes: n is input length; arithmetic on bounded machine integers is constant cost.

title: How do you analyze nested and consecutive loops?
answer: Add consecutive costs and multiply nested costs only after checking their bounds. A dependent inner bound may form a sum; two pointers that only advance can still take linear total work.
example: A loop over n customers containing a loop over m orders costs O(nm).
pitfall: Two syntactically nested loops are not automatically O(n²).
followUp: Analyze a pointer that advances across the input only once.

complexity.time: O(n + m) for separate scans; O(nm) for a full nested scan
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary if only counters are kept
complexity.notes: n and m are independent input sizes; no copied slices or hidden allocations.

title: State the invariant for binary search.
answer: Keep the possible answer inside a clearly defined interval, compare its middle and discard an impossible half. State whether endpoints are inclusive; compute mid as low + (high - low) / 2.
example: Find the first value at least a target using a half-open interval.
pitfall: Returning any matching duplicate does not implement lower bound.
followUp: How would you search a monotone feasibility function?

complexity.time: O(log n) comparisons
complexity.notes: Requires sorted random-access data or a monotone predicate; predicate cost multiplies the bound.

title: When can two pointers replace nested search?
answer: Exploit an invariant that tells you which pointer can move without losing a solution. In a sorted pair-sum search, a sum too small means the left value must increase.
example: Find a pair summing to a target in a sorted array.
pitfall: Sorting changes original indices unless you preserve them explicitly.
followUp: What if the input is unsorted and original indices are required?

complexity.time: Sorted scan O(n); sorting first adds O(n log n)
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary for scan, excluding sort workspace
complexity.notes: n is array length; sorted input is a precondition for this pointer rule.

title: When is a sliding window valid?
answer: Maintain a contiguous interval and an invariant that can be updated incrementally. The condition must tell you how shrinking affects validity; arbitrary negative values break some sum-based shrink rules.
example: Longest substring without repeated characters uses last-seen positions.
pitfall: The positive-only minimum-sum window algorithm is incorrect with unrestricted negatives.
followUp: Which data structure supports signed prefix sums instead?

complexity.time: Expected O(n) with hash-based last-seen tracking
complexity.notes: n is sequence length and u distinct symbols; define characters versus Unicode code points.

title: Why do prefix sums help range queries?
answer: Store cumulative totals so a range sum becomes the difference of two prefix totals. For target-sum subarray counting, a frequency map of earlier prefixes avoids enumerating every range.
example: Initialize frequency of prefix zero to one so ranges starting at index zero count.
pitfall: A set loses multiplicities when equal prefix totals occur repeatedly.
followUp: How do you handle many updates as well as queries?

complexity.time: Build O(n), each static range sum O(1); target count expected O(n)
complexity.space: O(n) prefix storage or frequency map
complexity.notes: Use a sufficiently wide numeric type; hash-map costs are expected.

title: Compare merge sort, quicksort and heapsort.
answer: Merge sort gives predictable n log n work and can be stable. Quicksort partitions in place but depends on pivot quality; heapsort gives worst-case n log n without linear merge workspace.
example: Choose a stable merge implementation when equal-key records must retain input order.
pitfall: Do not claim every library sort uses the same algorithm or workspace.
followUp: When can counting sort beat comparison sorting?

complexity.time: Merge O(n log n); randomized quicksort expected O(n log n), worst O(n²); heapsort O(n log n)
complexity.space: Array merge O(n); quicksort expected O(log n) recursion, worst O(n); iterative heapsort O(1)
complexity.notes: Comparison model; implementation and recursion strategy determine workspace.

title: When should you choose BFS over DFS?
answer: BFS finds minimum edge count from a source in an unweighted graph. DFS is useful for dependency structure, cycle reasoning and exhaustive exploration; both need visited tracking on general graphs.
example: Use BFS to find the fewest moves in an unweighted maze.
pitfall: Marking visited only on dequeue can enqueue duplicates unnecessarily.
followUp: Why does BFS fail as a shortest-path method for arbitrary weighted edges?

complexity.time: O(V + E) with adjacency lists
complexity.notes: V and E refer to the reachable graph or full traversal; BFS assumes equal edge weights.

title: Explain Dijkstra's invariant and its limitation.
answer: Repeatedly settle the unsettled vertex with smallest tentative distance and relax outgoing edges. Nonnegative weights make the settled distance final; negative edges invalidate that argument.
example: Find cheapest routes with nonnegative fares and a min-priority queue.
pitfall: A visited flag alone cannot fix Dijkstra for negative edges.
followUp: Which algorithm would you choose with negative edges?

complexity.time: O((V + E) log V) with an indexed binary heap
complexity.space: O(V + E) including graph, O(V) algorithm workspace
complexity.notes: A lazy heap storing duplicate entries instead uses O(E) heap space and O((V + E) log(V + E)) time.

title: How do you order tasks with dependencies?
answer: In Kahn's algorithm, enqueue zero-indegree vertices, remove them and decrement successors. If fewer than V vertices are emitted, a directed cycle prevents a full ordering.
example: Order build steps while allowing independent steps to run together.
pitfall: A valid ordering is not necessarily unique.
followUp: How would you report an actual cycle rather than only its presence?

complexity.time: O(V + E)
complexity.notes: Directed graph; count indegrees using the same edge multiplicities as traversal.

title: When is dynamic programming appropriate?
answer: Define states whose optimal values depend on smaller states, with overlapping subproblems and a valid recurrence. State the base cases and evaluation order before optimizing storage.
example: For climbing stairs, ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2) with defined starting cases.
pitfall: Memoizing an incorrect state definition does not make the recurrence correct.
followUp: Which states can be discarded after processing?

complexity.time: Stairs O(n) time
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary with two rolling values
complexity.notes: n is stair count; fixed-width arithmetic may overflow, while arbitrary-precision costs grow with digit length.

title: Why does 0/1 knapsack update capacity in descending order?
answer: A one-dimensional DP must read values from the previous item iteration. Descending capacity prevents the current item from being reused during its own update.
example: At capacity ten, one item of weight five can be selected only once.
pitfall: Ascending capacity solves an unbounded reuse variant instead.
followUp: Why is this called pseudopolynomial time?

complexity.time: O(nW)
complexity.notes: n items and integer capacity W; W is a numeric value, not its bit-length.

title: How do you analyze subset generation?
answer: At each position choose include or exclude, maintaining a partial choice and undoing it afterward. There are 2^n subsets; copying each output contributes up to n work.
example: Generate all subsets, including the empty subset.
pitfall: Reporting O(2^n) alone ignores materializing the elements of every subset.
followUp: How would duplicate inputs change generation?

complexity.time: O(n · 2^n) when materializing every subset
complexity.notes: n is input length; output storage is reported separately.

title: How do you justify a greedy algorithm?
answer: Prove that a locally chosen step can be part of an optimal solution, often by exchange argument, then show the remaining problem has the same structure.
example: For maximum nonoverlapping intervals, choose the earliest finishing interval next.
pitfall: A greedy rule that works for unweighted intervals need not solve weighted scheduling.
followUp: Give a counterexample to selecting the shortest interval.

complexity.time: O(n log n) sorting plus O(n) scan
complexity.space: O(n) sort workspace for a typical stable array sort; scan O(1)
complexity.notes: n intervals; output selection costs additional storage if retained.

title: How do you account for recursion and divide-and-conquer?
answer: Write the recurrence and count both work per level and depth. Include stack frames in auxiliary space even when no explicit collection is allocated.
example: Merge sort uses T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), giving logarithmically many linear-work levels.
pitfall: Depth O(log n) does not mean the whole algorithm is O(log n).
followUp: What changes if each recursive call copies its input slice?

complexity.time: Merge-sort recurrence O(n log n)
complexity.space: O(n) merge buffer plus O(log n) call stack
complexity.notes: Assume one reusable buffer; copying slices can change allocation volume.

title: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
answer: Java passes values. For an object variable, that value is a reference: a method can mutate the referenced object, but rebinding its parameter does not rebind the caller's variable.
example: A method can add to the caller's list, but assigning parameter = new ArrayList does not replace that caller's list.
pitfall: Describing Java as pass-by-reference obscures the distinction between mutation and reassignment.
followUp: What happens when the referenced object is immutable?

title: How do equals and hashCode work together?
answer: Equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal objects may collide. Override both for value-based keys and keep equality reflexive, symmetric, transitive and consistent.
example: An immutable OrderId value can safely key a map.
pitfall: Mutating a key's equality fields after insertion can make lookups fail.
followUp: How can inheritance break equals symmetry?

complexity.time: Hash-map lookup expected O(1) bucket work
complexity.notes: Hash/equality may themselves cost O(k) for keys containing k characters or fields.

title: Why is String immutable, and when use StringBuilder?
answer: Immutable strings can be safely shared and used as stable keys. A mutable builder avoids repeatedly copying a growing string inside a loop; it is not automatically safe for shared concurrent mutation.
example: Accumulate a CSV line in one builder, then call toString at the boundary.
pitfall: Repeated concatenation inside a growing loop may copy all earlier characters repeatedly.
followUp: How would you process Unicode code points rather than UTF-16 code units?

complexity.time: Builder construction O(L) total with amortized growth; repeated growing concatenation can be O(L²)
complexity.notes: L is total output length for bounded-size appended pieces.

title: Which Java collection fits a workload?
answer: Choose by required operations: ArrayList for indexed access, ArrayDeque for a stack/queue, HashMap for exact lookup and TreeMap for sorted navigation. Then consider null handling, iteration order and concurrency.
example: A FIFO work queue needs poll/offer semantics, not arbitrary list indexing.
pitfall: Selecting LinkedList solely because inserts are O(1) ignores lookup and allocation costs.
followUp: What would you measure before changing a hot collection?

complexity.time: ArrayList get O(1); deque end ops amortized O(1); TreeMap lookup O(log n)
complexity.notes: Single-threaded operations; allocations, key comparisons and contention can dominate real latency.

title: What do extends and super mean in generic APIs?
answer: A producer of T can be accepted as ? extends T, while a destination consuming T can be ? super T. Generic types are invariant; List<Integer> is not a subtype of List<Number>.
example: Copy numbers from a List<? extends Number> into a List<? super Number>.
pitfall: You generally cannot add arbitrary values to an extends wildcard because its actual element type is unknown.
followUp: How does type erasure affect overloads and runtime checks?

title: Checked or unchecked exception: how do you choose?
answer: Checked exceptions make callers acknowledge a recoverable contract at compile time; unchecked exceptions often represent programming errors or domain failures handled at a boundary. Preserve causes and translate at meaningful layers.
example: An API boundary maps a domain not-found exception to a documented response.
pitfall: Catching Exception and returning success destroys failure visibility.
followUp: When would try-with-resources preserve suppressed exceptions?

title: When are streams clearer than loops?
answer: Streams express transformations and reductions over a source. Keep operations free of shared side effects, understand laziness and short-circuiting, and use loops where control flow is clearer.
example: Filter invalid orders and sum amounts without mutating an external accumulator.
pitfall: Parallel streams do not guarantee lower latency and often use shared execution infrastructure.
followUp: Why must a reduction's combining operation be associative?

complexity.time: Filter/map/reduce O(n); sorted adds O(n log n)
complexity.space: O(1) incremental reduction, O(n) for sorting or collecting
complexity.notes: Assume constant-cost lambdas; retained output and stateful operations change space.

title: Does a final field make an object immutable?
answer: final prevents reassignment of that field after construction; it does not freeze a referenced list or array. Use encapsulation, defensive copies and immutable elements, and avoid leaking this during construction.
example: A record containing a mutable List still needs an appropriate copy policy.
pitfall: List.copyOf protects the list structure but does not deep-copy mutable elements.
followUp: What does safe publication guarantee for properly constructed final fields?

complexity.time: Defensive list copy O(n)
complexity.notes: n is list size; a deep-copy cost also depends on the reachable object graph.

title: volatile, synchronized or atomic variable?
answer: volatile provides visibility and ordering for a variable, but a read-modify-write increment is multiple actions. synchronized protects a critical section; atomics provide specific atomic operations such as compare-and-set.
example: Use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet for a shared counter rather than volatile count++.
pitfall: Thread-safe individual fields do not automatically preserve a multi-field invariant.
followUp: How would you update two account balances atomically?

title: Why is ConcurrentHashMap safer than sharing HashMap?
answer: It supports concurrent access with defined visibility guarantees. Use atomic per-key methods such as compute or merge for compound changes; arbitrary get-then-put sequences can still race.
example: Use merge(key, 1, Integer::sum) for independent per-key counts.
pitfall: A concurrent map does not make mutable values or a cross-key transfer atomic.
followUp: When should compute callbacks avoid blocking external work?

complexity.time: Expected O(1) simple key operations under good hashing
complexity.notes: Contention, resizing, key costs and callback work affect latency; this is not a lock-free timing guarantee.

title: How do you size and bound an executor?
answer: Separate CPU work from waiting work, bound accepted backlog and define rejection behavior. Measure queue time and service time; unbounded queues can turn overload into memory exhaustion.
example: Reject excess requests or apply backpressure rather than enqueueing indefinitely.
pitfall: Increasing threads does not increase database connection capacity.
followUp: How would you choose a timeout budget across queued and running work?

title: What do virtual threads solve and what do they not solve?
answer: They make many blocking tasks cheaper to represent, improving scalability for waiting-heavy workloads. They do not accelerate CPU-bound work or remove limits on connections, downstream services or shared locks.
example: Use one virtual thread per blocking request while bounding scarce database access with a semaphore.
pitfall: Java 21-era synchronized pinning advice is version-specific: JDK 24 removed that monitor limitation; native/foreign calls can still pin.
followUp: Which JDK version and blocking operations would you profile first?

title: How do you compose asynchronous work safely?
answer: Use thenCompose for dependent asynchronous stages and thenCombine for independent results. Choose executors deliberately, propagate exceptions and define timeouts and cancellation ownership.
example: Fetch independent inventory and price results before combining a quote.
pitfall: join inside an asynchronous pipeline can block a worker; a timeout does not necessarily cancel underlying I/O.
followUp: How would partial failure affect the response contract?

title: How do stack, heap and garbage collection relate?
answer: Each thread has execution frames; objects are generally managed on the heap, though optimizations can eliminate allocations. GC reclaims unreachable objects, so retained references can cause memory growth even without manual allocation leaks.
example: A static map retaining every request prevents those request graphs from becoming unreachable.
pitfall: Not every pause is GC; inspect allocation, threads, CPU and I/O evidence.
followUp: How would you distinguish a leak from an intentionally growing cache?

title: How would you diagnose a slow Java service?
answer: Start from latency distributions and traces, then inspect CPU samples, thread states, allocation and dependency timings. Form a hypothesis and measure before changing pool sizes or GC flags.
example: A request blocked on a database connection needs different treatment from a CPU-hot serialization loop.
pitfall: Optimizing a microbenchmark that excludes the bottleneck may not improve request latency.
followUp: What production-safe evidence would you capture during an incident?

title: What does Spring Boot add to Spring?
answer: Spring supplies dependency injection and application infrastructure. Boot adds opinionated auto-configuration, starters and operational conventions to reduce setup; it still uses Spring's container and APIs.
example: A web starter and matching classpath can configure a web application without manually wiring every infrastructure bean.
pitfall: Boot is not a replacement for understanding bean lifecycles or application configuration.
followUp: How would you inspect why an auto-configuration matched?

title: Why prefer constructor injection?
answer: Constructor injection declares required dependencies, supports straightforward unit testing and allows final fields. It also makes an excessive number of dependencies visible as a design smell.
example: Construct OrderService with an OrderRepository interface and a PaymentGateway.
pitfall: Field injection hides required collaborators and makes plain unit construction awkward.
followUp: What would a circular constructor dependency tell you about the design?

title: What is a bean scope and is singleton thread-safe?
answer: A singleton is normally one instance per bean definition per container. It says nothing about thread safety: request-specific mutable state should not be kept in an unprotected singleton field.
example: A stateless service can be shared; a currentCustomer field in that service can mix requests.
pitfall: Singleton does not mean one object across every process or every application context.
followUp: How would a request-scoped dependency be used from a singleton?

title: How does auto-configuration back off?
answer: Boot uses conditions on classpath, properties, application type and existing beans. User configuration can supply a bean that causes a conditional default to back off; inspect the condition report rather than guessing.
example: Defining a supported custom bean can replace an infrastructure default when its condition permits.
pitfall: A starter is a dependency bundle, not a guarantee that every related bean will be created.
followUp: How would you test a custom conditional auto-configuration?

title: How should you manage configuration and secrets?
answer: Bind related settings into validated ConfigurationProperties objects and understand property-source precedence. Supply secrets through deployment secret mechanisms and avoid committing or logging them.
example: Fail startup when a required endpoint or timeout is invalid.
pitfall: A profile name is not a security boundary; accidentally enabled diagnostics can still expose data.
followUp: How would you validate production configuration before rollout?

title: How do you design a clear REST controller?
answer: Keep transport parsing and response mapping in the controller, with business rules in application/domain services. Validate input, use appropriate status codes and document stable error shapes.
example: POST an order and return its identifier and Location when a new resource is created.
pitfall: Returning HTTP 200 for every failure forces clients to infer errors from ambiguous bodies.
followUp: How do you distinguish malformed input from a business conflict?

title: Where should validation happen?
answer: Validate request shape and constraints at the boundary, enforce domain invariants in the domain/service layer, and use database constraints for concurrent integrity. Map failures through consistent exception handling.
example: Validate a positive quantity, then atomically enforce inventory availability in storage.
pitfall: A pre-check alone cannot prevent two concurrent requests from violating uniqueness.
followUp: How would cross-field validation differ from field-level annotations?

title: What does Transactional actually intercept?
answer: With the usual proxy mode, an external call through the proxy gets transaction advice. A method calling another annotated method on the same instance bypasses that proxy; place the boundary deliberately or use an appropriate explicit mechanism.
example: Move the transactional operation into a separate collaborator invoked through its bean proxy.
pitfall: By default RuntimeException and Error trigger rollback; checked exceptions need suitable rollback rules unless defaults are customized.
followUp: How would you prove rollback with an integration test?

title: REQUIRED versus REQUIRES_NEW: what changes?
answer: REQUIRED joins an existing transaction or creates one. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the outer transaction and uses an independent transaction, usually needing another connection; its commit survives a later outer rollback.
example: An independent audit write may need a deliberately separate transaction and failure policy.
pitfall: An inner rollback-only mark can cause the outer REQUIRED commit to fail unexpectedly.
followUp: What happens if all pool connections are held by outer transactions?

title: How do you detect and fix an N+1 query problem?
answer: Inspect query counts for representative requests. Fetch associations deliberately with joins, entity graphs, batching or DTO queries; choose based on cardinality and pagination requirements.
example: Loading 50 orders and then each customer's data may issue many extra queries.
pitfall: Making every association eager can increase work and does not guarantee one efficient SQL query.
followUp: Why can collection fetch joins complicate pagination?

complexity.time: Naive N+1 uses 1 + n database round trips
complexity.notes: n is root records; SQL work, indexes, network latency and result size must be measured separately.

title: How do you prevent lost updates?
answer: Optimistic locking uses a version check and detects stale writes; pessimistic locking reserves database locks and can block competitors. Choose based on contention and transaction duration.
example: A versioned inventory update fails when another transaction has already changed that version.
pitfall: Blindly retrying a payment after a version conflict can duplicate external side effects.
followUp: How would you bound retries and handle a conflict for the caller?

title: How do authentication and authorization differ?
answer: Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides what that identity may do. Apply server-side checks to routes and business operations, validate tokens correctly and keep browser-specific CSRF assumptions explicit.
example: A valid token for user A must not allow reading user B's order.
pitfall: CORS is not authentication, and hiding a button does not authorize the API.
followUp: How would cookie-based sessions change CSRF protection needs?

title: Unit test, WebMvcTest or SpringBootTest?
answer: Use plain unit tests for isolated logic, a web slice for controller mapping/validation/security behavior, and a full application context for integration wiring. Use realistic database integration tests when SQL behavior matters.
example: A service unit test need not start the container; a rollback test should exercise the real transactional boundary.
pitfall: Mocking the repository cannot prove database constraints, query correctness or rollback semantics.
followUp: Which behavior requires a real external dependency instead of a mock?

title: How do timeouts, retries and idempotency fit together?
answer: Assign a total deadline, bound each dependency call and retry only transient failures within that budget. Backoff with jitter reduces synchronized retries; idempotency prevents repeated business effects.
example: Store an idempotency key and result for a payment request, with a defined retention period.
pitfall: Retries at every layer multiply traffic and can worsen an outage.
followUp: How do you handle a timeout when the remote side may have committed?

title: What makes a Boot application production-ready?
answer: Expose appropriately secured health and metrics, distinguish readiness from liveness, propagate trace context and design graceful shutdown. Observe latency, errors and saturation with bounded-cardinality labels.
example: Stop accepting new work before terminating while giving in-flight requests a bounded drain period.
pitfall: An unrestricted actuator endpoint or user IDs as metric labels can create operational and security problems.
followUp: When should a database outage affect readiness but not liveness?

title: What are encapsulation, abstraction and polymorphism?
answer: Encapsulation protects state and invariants. Abstraction exposes the capabilities callers need, while polymorphism lets implementations satisfy the same contract with different behavior.
example: A PaymentGateway contract hides provider-specific network details from checkout.
pitfall: Getters and setters for every field do not automatically produce meaningful encapsulation.
followUp: Where should payment validation live?

title: Composition or inheritance?
answer: Prefer composition when behavior should vary independently or the relationship is uses-a. Use inheritance only when subtypes genuinely honor the parent's behavioral contract and substitution remains safe.
example: A report service uses a formatter strategy rather than subclassing for every format/delivery combination.
pitfall: Reusing code through inheritance can expose methods that violate a subtype's invariants.
followUp: What changes when subclasses need incompatible preconditions?

title: How do you apply SOLID without overengineering?
answer: Keep responsibilities cohesive, depend on useful abstractions at change boundaries and preserve substitutable contracts. Apply interface segregation and extension points to actual variation rather than inventing a hierarchy for every class.
example: Separate price calculation from receipt delivery so either can change independently.
pitfall: One interface per class is not a goal; unnecessary indirection makes simple flows harder to follow.
followUp: Which likely change justifies an interface in your current design?

title: When should you use Strategy instead of conditionals?
answer: Use Strategy when alternative policies have a stable contract and evolve independently. A short, stable switch can be clearer when the choices are fixed; explain the change pressure before adding objects.
example: A ShippingCostPolicy computes a quote for a destination and package.
pitfall: A strategy that mutates unrelated shared state makes interchangeable behavior difficult to reason about.
followUp: How would you validate and select an allowed strategy?

title: Factory, builder or dependency injection?
answer: A factory encapsulates creation choices; a builder assembles a complex value with readable optional parameters. Dependency injection supplies collaborators and lifecycle ownership rather than being another name for any constructor.
example: A builder validates an immutable search request; a container wires the search service.
pitfall: Builders should not allow invalid objects to escape before validation.
followUp: How would you prevent callers from forgetting a required field?

title: What should an event publisher promise to subscribers?
answer: Specify delivery timing, ordering, failure isolation and subscription lifetime. In-process observer callbacks are not durable messaging and need explicit handling for slow or failing subscribers.
example: A UI model publishes changes and unregisters listeners when the view closes.
pitfall: One throwing callback should not accidentally prevent required cleanup or unrelated delivery.
followUp: When must an event move to a durable outbox/message broker?

complexity.time: Notify O(s) plus callback work
complexity.notes: s is subscribers; asynchronous delivery adds queue bounds and scheduling costs.

title: Design a parking lot from requirements.
answer: Clarify vehicle/space types, allocation, pricing and concurrency first. Model a ticket lifecycle, a spot repository and pricing policy; make spot reservation and ticket creation atomic within the chosen persistence boundary.
example: A ticket transitions from active to paid to exited with a defined policy for lost tickets.
pitfall: A class diagram alone does not prevent two attendants allocating the same spot.
followUp: How would EV charging or reservations change the model?

complexity.time: Indexed available-spot selection can be expected O(1) by type; scanning O(n)
complexity.notes: n is spots; database consistency and query plans determine real production cost.

title: How would you design an elevator controller?
answer: Separate car state, door safety, request queues and a scheduling policy. Define permitted transitions and hardware interlocks before optimizing routing; a local simulation cannot replace real safety systems.
example: A car must not move while its door-open interlock is active.
pitfall: Treating an elevator as a simple sorted list ignores direction, capacity and safety constraints.
followUp: How would emergency mode interrupt normal scheduling?

complexity.time: Ordered stop insertion/removal O(log n) with a balanced set
complexity.notes: n is queued stops for one car; selecting across cars needs its own cost model.

title: How do you model a vending machine with State?
answer: Represent legal transitions such as idle, funded, dispensing and refunding. Keep inventory and money invariants explicit and handle a dispense failure without pretending the sale succeeded.
example: Insufficient funds must not decrement inventory; a failed dispenser needs a refund/recovery policy.
pitfall: A collection of booleans permits impossible combinations like idle and dispensing together.
followUp: What happens if the process restarts after charging but before dispensing?

complexity.time: Indexed inventory lookup expected O(1)
complexity.notes: p is products; change-making algorithm cost is separate from state transitions.

title: Design a token-bucket rate limiter.
answer: Define capacity and refill rate, update tokens using elapsed monotonic time, then atomically consume if enough remain. Clarify whether limits apply per process, tenant or across a distributed fleet.
example: A capacity of ten allows a burst of ten while refilling at the configured rate.
pitfall: Unsynchronized read-check-write can grant the same tokens to multiple threads.
followUp: How do you bound memory for inactive users?

complexity.time: Expected O(1) per key update with hash lookup
complexity.notes: u is retained keys; distributed atomic storage adds network and contention costs.

title: Design a task scheduler with cancellation.
answer: Separate task identity, due time, execution ownership and lifecycle. Use a priority queue for next due time and define whether cancellation can prevent execution after a worker has claimed a task.
example: Cancellation before claim prevents execution; after claim it may only request cooperative interruption.
pitfall: Removing an arbitrary item from a basic heap is not automatically logarithmic.
followUp: What must change to survive a process crash?

complexity.time: Enqueue/pop O(log n); arbitrary cancel O(n) in a basic heap
complexity.notes: An indexed heap can support O(log n) removal; tombstones need bounded cleanup.

title: Design a booking workflow that prevents double booking.
answer: Define the availability interval, hold expiration and confirmation states. Use a storage-enforced uniqueness/exclusion rule or atomic conditional write, and make payment retries idempotent.
example: Two concurrent requests for the same seat cannot both confirm, even if both earlier reads saw it free.
pitfall: An in-memory lock on one application instance does not protect a multi-instance service.
followUp: How would you recover payment success followed by confirmation failure?

complexity.time: Depends on storage index and conflict detection; no universal O(1) guarantee
complexity.notes: Specify data model, index and isolation before assigning asymptotic costs.

title: How do you model money and time correctly?
answer: Use a money value object with amount, currency and explicit rounding rules. Represent instants and business time zones separately; use a clock abstraction for deterministic time-sensitive tests.
example: Two USD amounts can be added; adding USD to EUR requires an explicit conversion policy.
pitfall: Binary floating-point and a server-default time zone are unsafe defaults for many financial rules.
followUp: Where should tax rounding occur: line item or invoice total?

title: How do you make a stateful object thread-safe?
answer: State an invariant and identify the atomic boundary needed to preserve it. Choose confinement, immutability, locks or appropriate concurrent primitives; document ownership and avoid holding locks during slow external calls.
example: Protect both balance updates under a consistent lock order for an in-memory transfer.
pitfall: Concurrent collections do not make a sequence across several objects atomic.
followUp: How would you detect and prevent a lock-order deadlock?

title: How do you evaluate an object-oriented design in an interview?
answer: Walk a concrete use case through interfaces, state transitions, failures and tests. Evaluate cohesion, dependency direction and how likely changes affect the model; explain tradeoffs rather than naming patterns as the answer.
example: Add a second payment provider and trace which code must change and which contract tests stay valid.
pitfall: Presenting only the happy path misses concurrency, recovery and lifecycle responsibilities.
followUp: Which requirement would force the largest redesign, and why?
